topics.title: Database Concepts and Architecture
topics.summary: Why databases replaced file systems, the three-schema architecture, data independence, schemas versus instances, DBMS languages and the people who use them.

blocks.text:
## What a database system actually buys you

Before databases, every application kept its own files in its own format. That arrangement fails in five predictable ways, and the whole of DBMS theory is a response to those five failures.

**Redundancy and inconsistency.** The same student address sits in the hostel program's file and in the fee program's file. One gets updated, the other does not, and the two now disagree with no way to say which is right.

**Difficulty of access.** Each new question — "list students from Pune who owe fees" — needs a new program, because the file system offers only "read the next record".

**Integrity problems.** The rule "balance must not go below zero" lives inside application code. Add a sixth program and the rule has to be re-implemented, correctly, a sixth time.

**Atomicity problems.** A transfer debits one account and credits another. A crash between the two leaves money destroyed. Files have no notion of "both or neither".

**Concurrency and security problems.** Two clerks writing the same file interleave their writes; and a file either is readable or is not, with no way to say "this user may see salaries only for their own department".

A **database management system** is a layer that centralises the data and the rules about it, so all five problems are solved once rather than once per program. Everything else in this unit — constraints, transactions, normalization, views — is one of those solutions in detail.

## Data abstraction and the three-schema architecture

The core design idea, standardised as the ANSI/SPARC architecture, is to describe the same data at three levels at once.

| Level | Also called | Describes | Audience |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Internal** | physical schema | how bytes are stored: files, pages, indexes, compression | DB implementers, DBA tuning |
| **Conceptual** | logical schema | what entities, relations, attributes and constraints exist for the whole enterprise | database designer, DBA |
| **External** | view / subschema | one user group's partial, possibly restructured picture | application programmers, end users |

There is exactly **one** internal schema and exactly **one** conceptual schema for a database, but **many** external schemas. A university database has one conceptual schema containing `student`, `course`, `enrolment`, `faculty`, `salary`; the exam-cell view exposes marks without salaries; the payroll view exposes salaries without marks.

The DBMS is responsible for **mappings**: the external/conceptual mapping turns a query on a view into a query on the logical schema, and the conceptual/internal mapping turns that into file and index accesses. Every query pays the cost of two translations, which is exactly the price of the flexibility described next.

blocks.title: Three levels, two mappings, one purpose
blocks.text: Do not memorise the table as three words. Memorise the *shape*: external $\leftrightarrow$ conceptual $\leftrightarrow$ internal, with a mapping on each arrow. Each mapping absorbs a kind of change so the level above it does not have to notice. That is all data independence is.

## Physical and logical data independence

**Physical data independence** is the ability to change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema. Add a B+ tree index on `student.name`, switch from heap files to hash files, move a table to a faster disk, re-order fields inside a record — no application changes, no logical schema change. Only the conceptual/internal mapping is rewritten.

**Logical data independence** is the ability to change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas or the programs that use them. Add a new attribute to a relation, split a relation into two, add a whole new relation — and the existing views can be redefined so that the applications still see what they saw before. Only the external/conceptual mapping is rewritten.

Two facts are examined relentlessly:

1. **Logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical data independence.** Physical changes are invisible by construction, because the conceptual schema never mentions files or indexes. Logical changes are visible unless someone deliberately rewrites the view definitions to hide them — and some changes (dropping an attribute a view exposes) cannot be hidden at all.
2. **Each kind of independence is protected by one mapping only.** Physical independence lives in the conceptual/internal mapping; logical independence lives in the external/conceptual mapping. A question that says "which mapping must be changed when an index is added?" is asking for conceptual/internal.

blocks.title: Worked example — classifying six changes
blocks.text:
For each change, say which level changed, which mapping must be rewritten, and which kind of independence is being exercised.

| Change | Level changed | Mapping rewritten | Independence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create a hash index on `emp.eid` | internal | conceptual/internal | physical |
| Change `sal` from `NUMERIC(8,2)` to `NUMERIC(10,2)` in the logical schema | conceptual | external/conceptual | logical |
| Replace `emp(eid,name,dept,sal)` by `emp(eid,name,dept)` and `pay(eid,sal)` | conceptual | external/conceptual | logical |
| Move the `dept` table from a magnetic disk to SSD | internal | conceptual/internal | physical |
| Compress the records of a relation on disk | internal | conceptual/internal | physical |
| Add attribute `email` to `emp` | conceptual | external/conceptual | logical |

Check the third row carefully, because it is the classic exam item. Splitting a relation is a **logical** change. Existing applications that select `eid, name, sal` still work if we define a view

```sql
CREATE VIEW emp AS
  SELECT e.eid, e.name, e.dept, p.sal
  FROM   emp e NATURAL JOIN pay p;
```

so logical data independence has been *achieved* here — but only because someone wrote that view. If nobody does, the applications break. That is the precise sense in which logical independence is "harder": it requires work, whereas physical independence is automatic.

## Schema versus instance, and the data models

The **schema** is the description — the set of relation names, attributes, domains and constraints. It is set at design time and changes rarely. The **instance** (or state, or snapshot) is the set of rows present at one moment. It changes with every `INSERT`. The analogy with programming is exact: schema is to instance as a type declaration is to the value of a variable.

A **data model** is the collection of concepts used to write a schema, together with operations and constraints. The historically important ones:

- **Hierarchical** (IBM IMS): records in a tree, parent-to-child one-to-many links. Many-to-many relationships need duplicated records.
- **Network** (CODASYL/DBTG): records in a graph of owner–member sets. Handles many-to-many, but navigation is pointer-chasing done by the programmer.
- **Relational** (Codd, 1970): data as mathematical relations — unordered sets of tuples over named attributes — with declarative query languages. The programmer says *what*, not *how*.
- **Object-oriented and object-relational**: adds user-defined types, inheritance and methods.
- **Entity–Relationship model**: strictly a *conceptual design* model, not an implementation model. You design in ER and then map to relational.
- **Semi-structured / XML / JSON document models**: the schema travels with the data, and different records may have different attributes.

The key distinction to keep is **record-based** (hierarchical, network, relational — fixed record types) versus **object-based** (ER, OO, semantic — richer structures for design).

## DBMS languages and their sublanguages

- **DDL** — Data Definition Language: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`. Output goes into the **data dictionary** (system catalogue), which is itself stored as tables. DDL statements in SQL are auto-committed.
- **DML** — Data Manipulation Language: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`. Split into **procedural** DML (say what data and how to get it — relational algebra is the model here) and **declarative / non-procedural** DML (say what data only — relational calculus and SQL).
- **DCL** — Data Control Language: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`.
- **TCL** — Transaction Control: `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`.
- **VDL** — View Definition Language, used to specify external schemas. In SQL this is just `CREATE VIEW`, part of DDL.
- **SDL** — Storage Definition Language, for the internal schema. Modern systems fold it into DDL clauses such as `CREATE INDEX` or tablespace options.

A **data sublanguage** such as SQL is embedded in a host language (C, Java) because it is not computationally complete on its own; the mismatch between set-at-a-time SQL and record-at-a-time host loops is the **impedance mismatch**, handled by cursors.

## People, components and architectures

The **DBA** designs the conceptual and internal schemas, grants authorisation, defines the storage structure, and handles backup and tuning. **Database designers** produce the conceptual schema; **application programmers** write against external schemas; **naive end users** use canned transactions such as an ATM menu; **sophisticated users** write their own queries.

Inside the engine, two halves: the **query processor** (DDL interpreter, DML compiler, query optimiser, evaluation engine) and the **storage manager** (authorisation and integrity manager, transaction manager, file manager, buffer manager). Persistent structures on disk are data files, the data dictionary, indexes and statistical data.

Deployment shapes appear as short questions:

- **Two-tier**: application/client speaks directly to the DBMS server (ODBC/JDBC). Business logic sits on the client.
- **Three-tier**: client $\to$ application server $\to$ database server. Better scaling and security, because the client never holds a database connection or credentials. Web applications are three-tier.
- **Centralised, client–server, parallel, distributed** are the classic system-architecture list; distributed databases get their own treatment in topic 4.7.

blocks.q: A DBA reorganises a relation from a heap file into a clustered B+ tree on the primary key. No application program needs to change. This demonstrates
blocks.exp: File organisation and indexing belong to the internal (physical) schema. Changing it and having the conceptual schema and all programs remain valid is precisely physical data independence; only the conceptual/internal mapping is rewritten.

blocks.q: Which of the following is TRUE of the three-schema architecture?
opts: There is one external schema and many conceptual schemas
There is one conceptual schema and many external schemas
There are many internal schemas, one per user
Conceptual and internal schemas are the same thing under different names
blocks.exp: One internal schema describes storage, one conceptual schema describes the whole enterprise's logical content, and each user group gets its own external schema (view). Multiple external schemas over a single conceptual schema is the arrangement that makes logical data independence and view-level security possible.

blocks.q: `GRANT SELECT ON emp TO clerk;` belongs to which sublanguage?
blocks.exp: `GRANT` and `REVOKE` control access privileges and form the Data Control Language. `CREATE`/`ALTER`/`DROP` are DDL, `SELECT`/`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` are DML, and `COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK`/`SAVEPOINT` are TCL.

tricks.title: Read the level off the vocabulary of the change
tricks.body: If the sentence contains *index, file, block, page, compression, disk, pointer, storage*, it is **internal** $\Rightarrow$ physical independence. If it contains *attribute, relation, table, constraint, split, merge*, it is **conceptual** $\Rightarrow$ logical independence. This one-word test answers almost every data-independence question without thinking about mappings.

tricks.title: Count the schemas: 1, 1, many
tricks.body: Internal = 1, conceptual = 1, external = many. Any option claiming many conceptual or many internal schemas is wrong on sight, and any option claiming one external schema is wrong too.

tricks.title: Mapping = the arrow you crossed
tricks.body: Name the two levels the change sits between and you have named the mapping. Storage change $\Rightarrow$ conceptual/internal. Logical change $\Rightarrow$ external/conceptual. Never say 'both mappings' unless the change genuinely rewrites the logical schema *and* its storage.

tricks.title: ER is a design model, not an implementation model
tricks.body: In any 'which of these is a record-based data model' question, ER is the odd one out along with object-oriented and semantic models. Hierarchical, network and relational are record-based.

tricks.title: Schema : instance :: type : value
tricks.body: When a question asks what changes frequently, it is the instance; what is compiled once and stored in the data dictionary is the schema. The *intension* is the schema, the *extension* is the instance.

traps.title: Logical independence is the harder one
traps.body: Candidates reverse this because 'physical' sounds harder. It is the opposite: physical changes are invisible to the logical schema by construction, while logical changes are visible unless view definitions are deliberately rewritten — and some cannot be hidden at all. Relational systems provide good physical independence and only partial logical independence.

traps.title: Adding a view is not logical data independence by itself
traps.body: Data independence is about *insulating existing users from a change*. Creating a brand-new view for a brand-new user is not independence; redefining an existing view so that old programs survive a schema change is.

traps.title: Data dictionary versus data
traps.body: The catalogue stores the schema (metadata), not the rows. A question asking 'where is the description of the database stored' wants the data dictionary / system catalogue, not the internal schema and not the database itself.

traps.title: TRUNCATE is DDL, DELETE is DML
traps.body: Both remove rows, but `TRUNCATE` deallocates storage, cannot be rolled back in most systems, and is classified as DDL; `DELETE` is a row-at-a-time logged DML operation that can be rolled back and can carry a `WHERE` clause.

topics.title: ER Modeling and the Relational Model
topics.summary: Entities, attributes, relationship degree and cardinality, weak entities, participation, EER generalisation, and the mechanical rules for mapping an ER diagram to relations — plus keys and integrity constraints.

blocks.text:
## The purpose of an ER diagram

The ER model is a *design* notation. You use it to argue with the client about what the world contains before you commit to tables, because changing a diagram is cheap and changing a live schema is not. Its only three primitives are **entities** (things with independent existence), **attributes** (properties of things) and **relationships** (associations among things).

An **entity type** is the schema-level description (`STUDENT`, with attributes `roll`, `name`, `dob`); an **entity** is one instance; the **entity set** is the current collection. The same intension/extension distinction as schema versus instance.

Attributes come in kinds that matter for mapping:

- **Simple** versus **composite** — `name` decomposing into `first`, `last`.
- **Single-valued** versus **multivalued** — `phone` may hold several values, drawn with a double ellipse.
- **Stored** versus **derived** — `age` derived from `dob`, drawn with a dashed ellipse.
- **Key attribute** — underlined; uniquely identifies entities of the type.
- **Complex** — composite of multivalued of composite, e.g. `address_phone`.

A **NULL** value means one of two different things — *not applicable* (a `spouse_name` for an unmarried person) or *unknown* (a phone number that exists but was not recorded). The relational model cannot tell them apart, which is where most NULL trouble in topic 4.4 comes from.

## Relationships: degree, roles, cardinality, participation

A **relationship type** $R$ among entity types $E_1, \ldots, E_n$ is a set of $n$-tuples. The number $n$ is the **degree**: degree 2 is **binary**, degree 3 **ternary**, degree 1 **unary** or **recursive** (`EMPLOYEE supervises EMPLOYEE`, where the two ends need **role names** `supervisor` and `supervisee` to be distinguishable).

**Cardinality ratio** constrains how many entities of one type may participate. For binary relationships the four cases are $1{:}1$, $1{:}N$, $N{:}1$ and $M{:}N$. Read them carefully: in `EMPLOYEE manages DEPARTMENT` with ratio $1{:}1$, one employee manages at most one department and one department has at most one manager.

**Participation** says whether *every* entity must take part.

- **Total participation** (existence dependency), drawn with a **double line**: every `DEPARTMENT` must have a manager.
- **Partial participation**, single line: not every `EMPLOYEE` manages.

The two constraints are independent and combine into the **(min, max)** notation written on the edge next to an entity: `EMPLOYEE (0,1) manages (1,1) DEPARTMENT` means each employee manages between 0 and 1 departments, each department has exactly 1 manager. Note the reversal convention — in (min,max) the pair sits beside the entity it constrains, whereas the cardinality-ratio label $1{:}N$ sits in the diamond. Mis-reading which side the $N$ belongs to is the commonest diagram error.

Relationships may have their own **attributes**. `WORKS_ON` between `EMPLOYEE` and `PROJECT` carries `hours`. For an $M{:}N$ relationship the attribute *must* live on the relationship; for $1{:}N$ it can be migrated to the $N$-side entity.

## Weak entity types

A **weak entity type** has no key attribute of its own. It is identified only in combination with an entity of its **identifying (owner) entity type**, through an **identifying relationship**. `DEPENDENT` is the standard example: two employees may each have a daughter named Anjali born on the same date, so `(name, dob)` is not unique across the company; it is unique only *within one employee*.

Notation: double rectangle for the weak entity, double diamond for the identifying relationship, dashed underline for the **partial key** (discriminator). Two properties always hold:

1. The weak entity has **total participation** in the identifying relationship — it cannot exist without an owner.
2. The identifying relationship is $1{:}N$ from owner to weak entity (an owner has many dependents; a dependent has one owner).

The primary key of the weak entity, after mapping, is *owner's primary key + partial key*.

A common exam distinction: an entity that merely has total participation in some relationship is **not** thereby weak. Weakness is about *identification*, not about existence. `EMPLOYEE` may be totally participating in `WORKS_FOR` yet still have its own key `ssn`, so it is strong.

## Enhanced ER: generalisation, specialisation, aggregation

**Specialisation** takes an entity type and defines subclasses by some distinguishing characteristic: `EMPLOYEE` specialises into `SECRETARY`, `ENGINEER`, `TECHNICIAN`. **Generalisation** is the same structure discovered bottom-up: noticing that `CAR` and `TRUCK` share attributes and inventing `VEHICLE`. Subclasses **inherit** all attributes of the superclass plus its relationship participations. The relationship between a subclass and its superclass is the **IS-A** relationship.

Two orthogonal constraints:

- **Disjointness**: **disjoint** ($d$) — an entity belongs to at most one subclass; **overlapping** ($o$) — it may belong to several. A person may be both a student and an employee: overlapping.
- **Completeness**: **total** (double line to the circle) — every superclass entity must belong to some subclass; **partial** — some belong to none.

That gives four combinations: disjoint-total, disjoint-partial, overlapping-total, overlapping-partial.

A **union type** or **category** is a subclass of the *union* of several superclasses: `OWNER` is a category over `PERSON`, `BANK`, `COMPANY`. Unlike a shared subclass (multiple inheritance), a category member inherits from only the one superclass it actually came from.

**Aggregation** treats a whole relationship as if it were an entity so that another relationship can point at it — needed when, for example, a `MANAGES` relationship between `EMPLOYEE` and `PROJECT` must itself be related to `MACHINERY` that is used for that management. Without aggregation you would need a ternary relationship, which asserts a different (and usually wrong) constraint.

## The relational model and its keys

A **relation schema** $R(A_1, \ldots, A_n)$ has a **domain** for each attribute. A **relation instance** is a *set* of tuples — so there is no ordering of tuples, no ordering of attributes (they are named), no duplicate tuples, and every value is **atomic** (first normal form is built into the definition). SQL tables violate two of these — they are multisets and their columns are positionally ordered — which is a favourite "which statement is false" item.

Key vocabulary, from loosest to tightest:

- **Superkey** — any set of attributes whose values are unique across tuples. $R$ itself is always a superkey.
- **Candidate key** — a minimal superkey: no proper subset is a superkey.
- **Primary key** — the one candidate key chosen by the designer; it may not be NULL.
- **Alternate key** — the candidate keys not chosen.
- **Foreign key** — attributes of $R_1$ whose values must appear as the primary-key value of some tuple of $R_2$, or be entirely NULL.
- **Composite key** — any key with more than one attribute. **Prime attribute** — an attribute belonging to *some* candidate key.

If a relation has $n$ attributes and $k$ candidate keys, the number of superkeys is computed by inclusion–exclusion over the candidate keys; the simplest case, one candidate key of size $m$ in a relation of $n$ attributes, gives $2^{\,n-m}$ superkeys.

## Integrity constraints

**Domain constraint.** Each attribute value must be an atomic value from its declared domain.

**Key constraint.** No two tuples of a relation may agree on a candidate key.

**Entity integrity.** No attribute of a **primary key** may be NULL. (Other candidate keys declared `UNIQUE` *may* be NULL in SQL, which is why `UNIQUE` and `PRIMARY KEY` are not synonyms.)

**Referential integrity.** If $R_1.FK$ references $R_2.PK$ then for every tuple of $R_1$, either $FK$ is wholly NULL or there is a tuple of $R_2$ with that PK value. Violations are prevented on `INSERT`/`UPDATE` of the child and on `DELETE`/`UPDATE` of the parent, where SQL offers `NO ACTION`/`RESTRICT`, `CASCADE`, `SET NULL` and `SET DEFAULT`.

**Semantic (business) constraints** — "an employee's salary must not exceed their manager's" — cannot be expressed by the above and need `CHECK`, assertions or triggers.

Which operations can violate what is worth a table:

| Operation | Can violate |
|---|---|
| `INSERT` into child | domain, key, entity, referential |
| `DELETE` from parent | referential only |
| `UPDATE` of a non-key attribute | domain only |
| `UPDATE` of a primary key | key, entity, referential (both sides) |

Note the row that is examined most: a plain `DELETE` can never violate domain, key or entity integrity — only referential integrity, and only if it removes a referenced parent.

## Mapping ER to relations: the seven steps

This algorithm is mechanical and is examined as "how many tables does this diagram need?".

1. **Strong entity type $E$** $\to$ one relation with all simple attributes; composite attributes contribute their leaf components; choose a key attribute as primary key.
2. **Weak entity type $W$ with owner $E$** $\to$ one relation containing $W$'s attributes plus $E$'s primary key as a foreign key; primary key = owner key + partial key; the foreign key gets `ON DELETE CASCADE`.
3. **Binary $1{:}1$ relationship** $\to$ no new relation. Put the other side's primary key as a foreign key into the relation of the entity with **total participation** (fewer NULLs). If both are total, consider merging the two entities into one relation.
4. **Binary $1{:}N$ relationship** $\to$ no new relation. Put the primary key of the **1-side** into the relation of the **N-side** as a foreign key, plus any relationship attributes.
5. **Binary $M{:}N$ relationship** $\to$ a **new relation** whose attributes are the two foreign keys plus the relationship attributes; primary key = the two foreign keys together.
6. **Multivalued attribute** $\to$ a **new relation** holding the attribute plus the owner's primary key; primary key = both together.
7. **$n$-ary relationship, $n \ge 3$** $\to$ a new relation with all $n$ foreign keys; primary key is the combination of foreign keys from the participants that do **not** have cardinality 1.

For EER specialisation there are four mapping options: (a) one relation per subclass plus one for the superclass; (b) relations for subclasses only (valid only when the specialisation is total and disjoint); (c) one single relation with a type attribute (good for disjoint); (d) one single relation with several Boolean type flags (needed for overlapping).

**The counting rule**: number of relations $=$ (strong entities) $+$ (weak entities) $+$ ($M{:}N$ relationships) $+$ (multivalued attributes) $+$ ($n$-ary relationships). $1{:}1$ and $1{:}N$ relationships add **zero** tables.

blocks.title: Worked example — mapping a small company diagram
blocks.text:
The diagram:

- `EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, {phone}, address(house, city))` — `phone` multivalued, `address` composite.
- `DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname)`.
- `PROJECT(pnumber, pname)`.
- `DEPENDENT(dep_name, dob)` — weak, owned by `EMPLOYEE` via identifying relationship `HAS`.
- `WORKS_FOR`: `EMPLOYEE` $N$ : 1 `DEPARTMENT`, employee total.
- `MANAGES`: `EMPLOYEE` 1 : 1 `DEPARTMENT`, department total.
- `WORKS_ON`: `EMPLOYEE` $M$ : $N$ `PROJECT`, with attribute `hours`.
- `SUPERVISES`: recursive 1 : $N$ on `EMPLOYEE`.

**Count first.** Strong entities 3, weak entities 1, $M{:}N$ relationships 1, multivalued attributes 1, $n$-ary 0. Total $= 3+1+1+1+0 = \mathbf{6}$ relations. `WORKS_FOR`, `MANAGES` and `SUPERVISES` add none.

**The schemas.**

```
EMPLOYEE(ssn, name, house, city, dno, super_ssn)
      dno      -> DEPARTMENT(dnumber)      [step 4, 1:N: key of 1-side goes to N-side]
      super_ssn-> EMPLOYEE(ssn)            [step 4 on a recursive 1:N]

DEPARTMENT(dnumber, dname, mgr_ssn)
      mgr_ssn  -> EMPLOYEE(ssn)            [step 3, 1:1: FK goes to the TOTAL side,
                                            which is DEPARTMENT]

EMP_PHONE(ssn, phone)                      [step 6; PK = both attributes]
      ssn      -> EMPLOYEE(ssn)

DEPENDENT(ssn, dep_name, dob)              [step 2; PK = (ssn, dep_name)]
      ssn      -> EMPLOYEE(ssn) ON DELETE CASCADE

PROJECT(pnumber, pname)

WORKS_ON(ssn, pnumber, hours)              [step 5; PK = (ssn, pnumber)]
```

Two details worth pausing on. The composite attribute `address` became two ordinary columns `house` and `city` — composite attributes never create a table. And `MANAGES` put its foreign key in `DEPARTMENT`, not `EMPLOYEE`: had we put `manages_dnumber` into `EMPLOYEE`, it would be NULL for every non-manager, whereas `mgr_ssn` in `DEPARTMENT` is never NULL because department participation is total.

blocks.q: An ER diagram has 4 strong entity types, 1 weak entity type, 3 relationships with ratio 1:N, 2 with ratio M:N, and one multivalued attribute. Assuming no relation merging, the minimum number of relations is
blocks.exp: Count 4 (strong) + 1 (weak) + 2 (M:N) + 1 (multivalued) = 8. The three 1:N relationships are absorbed as foreign keys on their N-sides and create no relations.

blocks.q: Which of the following statements about weak entity types is FALSE?
opts: A weak entity has total participation in its identifying relationship
The partial key alone is not sufficient to identify a weak entity
A weak entity type may have a candidate key of its own
The identifying relationship is 1:N from owner to weak entity
blocks.exp: Having a key of its own is exactly what makes an entity strong. The other three are definitional: a weak entity cannot exist without an owner (total participation), it is identified by owner key plus partial key, and one owner identifies many weak entities.

blocks.q: Which operation can violate ONLY the referential integrity constraint and nothing else?
blocks.exp: Deleting a tuple removes data, so it can never create a duplicate key, a NULL primary key or an out-of-domain value. It can only orphan child tuples that referenced the deleted parent, which is a referential-integrity violation.

tricks.title: Only four things create tables
tricks.body: Weak entities, $M{:}N$ relationships, multivalued attributes and $n$-ary ($n\ge3$) relationships. Strong entities create one each, and $1{:}1$ / $1{:}N$ relationships create none. Count those five buckets and you have the answer to every 'how many relations' question in seconds.

tricks.title: Foreign key goes to the 'many' side, or to the 'total' side
tricks.body: For $1{:}N$ the FK always lands on the $N$-side — there is exactly one value to store there. For $1{:}1$ there is a choice, and the rule is to put it on the side with **total participation**, because that column is then never NULL.

tricks.title: Read (min,max) as 'this entity participates in between min and max relationship instances'
tricks.body: min $=1$ means total participation; min $=0$ means partial. And the (min,max) pair is placed on the *same* side as the entity it describes, which is the opposite convention from the $1{:}N$ label in the diamond — so a $1{:}N$ relationship shows $(1,1)$ next to the $N$-side entity.

tricks.title: Superkey count from one candidate key
tricks.body: With $n$ attributes and a single candidate key of size $m$, every superkey is that key plus any subset of the remaining $n-m$ attributes, giving $2^{\,n-m}$ superkeys. With two candidate keys use inclusion–exclusion: $2^{n-m_1} + 2^{n-m_2} - 2^{n-|K_1 \cup K_2|}$.

tricks.title: Total participation does not mean weak
tricks.body: Ask only one question to classify an entity as weak: *does it have a key of its own?* If yes it is strong no matter how total its participation is. If no, it is weak and it will need its owner's key.

traps.title: Composite attributes never make a table, multivalued always do
traps.body: `address(street, city, pin)` becomes three columns in the same relation. `{phone}` becomes a new relation with the owner's key. Candidates routinely swap these, inflating or deflating the table count by one.

traps.title: $M{:}N$ relationship attributes cannot be migrated
traps.body: `hours` in `WORKS_ON` has no home in `EMPLOYEE` or `PROJECT` — a given employee has a different `hours` for each project. In a $1{:}N$ relationship an attribute *can* migrate to the $N$-side, and examiners test whether you know the difference.

traps.title: Cardinality ratio labels are read across the diamond
traps.body: In `EMPLOYEE 1 --- WORKS_FOR --- N DEPARTMENT`, the $N$ next to `DEPARTMENT` does not mean 'a department has many employees'; in the standard Chen convention it means one employee is related to $N$ departments. Different textbooks place the labels differently, so always resolve the ambiguity from the sentence given, not from the letter.

traps.title: UNIQUE is not PRIMARY KEY
traps.body: Entity integrity forbids NULL in the primary key only. A `UNIQUE` column in SQL may contain NULLs — and, because NULL is never equal to NULL, may contain several of them in most implementations. A question asking which constraint prevents NULLs is asking about entity integrity or an explicit `NOT NULL`.

topics.title: Relational Algebra and Relational Calculus
topics.summary: The six basic operators and the derived ones, division in full, join varieties and their cardinalities, and tuple and domain calculus with safety.

blocks.text:
## Why two query languages

Codd gave the relational model two equivalent query languages so that the model could be both *implemented* and *reasoned about*.

**Relational algebra** is **procedural**: a query is an expression built from operators, and the expression itself describes an evaluation order. This is what a query optimiser manipulates, so algebra is the language of query processing.

**Relational calculus** is **declarative**: a query is a logical formula describing which tuples belong in the answer, with no hint of how to compute them. SQL's `SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE` is modelled on tuple calculus.

Codd's theorem says the two are equivalent in expressive power: every algebra expression has a safe calculus formula and vice versa. A language at least as expressive as relational algebra is called **relationally complete**. SQL is relationally complete and, with grouping, aggregation and recursion, strictly more expressive — plain relational algebra has no aggregates, no arithmetic and no transitive closure.

## The six basic operators

Every other operator is shorthand for a combination of these.

| Operator | Symbol | Arity | Result schema |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selection | $\sigma_{\text{cond}}(R)$ | unary | same as $R$ |
| Projection | $\pi_{A_1,\ldots,A_k}(R)$ | unary | $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ |
| Union | $R \cup S$ | binary | same as $R$ (union-compatible) |
| Set difference | $R - S$ | binary | same as $R$ |
| Cartesian product | $R \times S$ | binary | all attributes of both |
| Rename | $\rho_{S(B_1,\ldots,B_n)}(R)$ | unary | renamed |

**Selection** keeps rows; its condition uses $=, \ne, <, \le, >, \ge$ combined with $\wedge, \vee, \neg$. It is *commutative*: $\sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R)) = \sigma_{c_2}(\sigma_{c_1}(R)) = \sigma_{c_1 \wedge c_2}(R)$.

**Projection** keeps columns and — because a relation is a set — **removes duplicates**. This is the single biggest behavioural difference from SQL, where `SELECT` keeps duplicates unless you write `DISTINCT`. Consequently $|\pi_A(R)| \le |R|$, with equality only when $A$ contains a superkey.

**Union, intersection and difference** require **union compatibility**: the same number of attributes, with pairwise compatible domains. Attribute *names* need not match; positions and domains must.

Cardinality bounds worth memorising: $\max(|R|,|S|) \le |R \cup S| \le |R|+|S|$; $0 \le |R \cap S| \le \min(|R|,|S|)$; $|R|-|S| \le |R-S| \le |R|$ (lower bound floored at 0); $|R \times S| = |R| \cdot |S|$ exactly.

## Derived operators

**Intersection.** $R \cap S = R - (R - S)$. Definable, hence not basic.

**Theta join.** $R \bowtie_\theta S = \sigma_\theta(R \times S)$. When $\theta$ is a conjunction of equalities it is an **equijoin**, and the join column then appears **twice** in the result.

**Natural join.** $R \bowtie S$ equijoins on *all* commonly named attributes and keeps **one copy** of each. If $R$ and $S$ share no attribute names, the natural join degenerates to the Cartesian product — a favourite trick question. Natural join is associative and commutative (up to attribute order).

**Outer joins** keep the tuples that the inner join would discard, padding with NULL.

- **Left outer** $R ⟕ S$: all of $R$, matched or not.
- **Right outer** $R ⟖ S$: all of $S$.
- **Full outer** $R ⟗ S$: all of both.

**Semijoin** $R ⋉ S = \pi_{\text{attr}(R)}(R \bowtie S)$ — the tuples of $R$ that have a partner. Important in distributed query processing because it ships only the join column.

**Division** $R \div S$ is the algebraic "for all". If $R$ has attributes $X \cup Y$ and $S$ has attributes $Y$, then

$$R \div S = \{\, t \text{ over } X \;\mid\; \forall s \in S,\; (t \cup s) \in R \,\}$$

Its expansion in basic operators, which you should be able to reproduce, is

$$R \div S \;=\; \pi_X(R) \;-\; \pi_X\big( (\pi_X(R) \times S) - R \big)$$

Read the right-hand side as: take all candidate $X$ values; form every pairing they *would* need; subtract the pairings that actually exist; anything left is a missing requirement, so remove those candidates.

blocks.title: Worked example — division, computed twice
blocks.text:
`ENROLLED(student, course)`:

| student | course |
|---|---|
| Amit | DB |
| Amit | OS |
| Amit | CN |
| Bina | DB |
| Chirag | DB |
| Chirag | OS |
| Deepa | DB |
| Deepa | OS |
| Deepa | CN |
| Deepa | AI |

`CORE(course)` = {DB, OS, CN}. Query: *students enrolled in every core course*, i.e. $\text{ENROLLED} \div \text{CORE}$.

**By definition.** Amit has {DB, OS, CN} $\supseteq$ core: yes. Bina has {DB}: no. Chirag has {DB, OS}, missing CN: no. Deepa has {DB, OS, CN, AI} $\supseteq$ core: yes — the extra AI is irrelevant, division asks for *at least* all of $S$. Answer: **{Amit, Deepa}**.

**By the formula.** 
- $\pi_{\text{student}}(\text{ENROLLED}) = \{$Amit, Bina, Chirag, Deepa$\}$, so 4 candidates.
- $\pi_{\text{student}}(\text{ENROLLED}) \times \text{CORE}$ has $4 \times 3 = 12$ tuples: every student paired with DB, OS and CN.
- Subtract ENROLLED. Which of the 12 are absent from ENROLLED? Amit: all three present. Bina: has DB, so (Bina,OS) and (Bina,CN) survive. Chirag: has DB and OS, so (Chirag,CN) survives. Deepa: all three present. The difference is $\{(\text{Bina},\text{OS}), (\text{Bina},\text{CN}), (\text{Chirag},\text{CN})\}$ — note that (Deepa, AI) never enters, because AI is not in $S$ and so was never in the product.
- $\pi_{\text{student}}$ of that difference $=\{$Bina, Chirag$\}$.
- Final: $\{$Amit, Bina, Chirag, Deepa$\} - \{$Bina, Chirag$\} = \{$**Amit, Deepa**$\}$. The two methods agree.

**Degree and cardinality.** $\deg(R \div S) = \deg(R) - \deg(S) = 2 - 1 = 1$. Cardinality is at most $|\pi_X(R)| = 4$, and here it is 2.

## Join cardinalities you should be able to bound

Let $R$ have $r$ tuples, $S$ have $s$ tuples, and let them share attribute set $Y$.

- **No common attribute**: natural join $=$ Cartesian product, exactly $r \cdot s$ tuples.
- **$Y$ is a key of $S$ and a foreign key of $R$ (declared `NOT NULL`)**: each $R$ tuple matches exactly one $S$ tuple, so the natural join has exactly $r$ tuples.
- **$Y$ a key of neither**: between $0$ and $r \cdot s$.
- **Left outer join**: between $r$ and $r\cdot s$; it is exactly $r$ when $Y$ is a key of $S$.
- **Full outer join**: at least $\max(r,s)$, at most $r + s$ when nothing matches at all.

A frequent numerical asks for the *minimum* size of a full outer join given that the inner join has $k$ tuples: it is $k + (\text{unmatched } R) + (\text{unmatched } S)$, and the minimum over all instances is $\max(r,s)$.

## Tuple relational calculus

A TRC query has the form

$$\{\, t \mid P(t) \,\}$$

where $t$ is a **tuple variable** and $P$ is a first-order formula built from atoms $t \in R$, $t.A \;\theta\; u.B$ and $t.A \;\theta\; c$, using $\wedge, \vee, \neg, \Rightarrow$ and the quantifiers $\exists t$ and $\forall t$.

*All employees earning more than 50000:*
$$\{\, t \mid t \in \text{EMP} \wedge t.sal > 50000 \,\}$$

*Names of employees in the department located in Pune:*
$$\{\, t \mid \exists e \in \text{EMP}\, \exists d \in \text{DEPT} \;( e.dept = d.dept \wedge d.city = \text{'Pune'} \wedge t.name = e.name ) \,\}$$

*Students enrolled in every core course* — the calculus version of division uses $\forall$ directly:
$$\{\, t \mid \exists e \in \text{ENROLLED}\,(t.student = e.student) \wedge \forall c \in \text{CORE}\;\big(\exists f \in \text{ENROLLED}\,(f.student = t.student \wedge f.course = c.course)\big) \,\}$$

The universal quantifier can always be eliminated by $\forall x\, P \equiv \neg \exists x\, \neg P$, which is exactly how SQL expresses division with `NOT EXISTS ... NOT EXISTS`.

## Domain relational calculus and safety

DRC uses one variable per **attribute** rather than per tuple:

$$\{\, \langle x_1, \ldots, x_n \rangle \mid P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \,\}$$

*Names of employees earning more than 50000:*
$$\{\, \langle n \rangle \mid \exists i, d, s\; ( \langle i, n, d, s \rangle \in \text{EMP} \wedge s > 50000 ) \,\}$$

QBE is based on domain calculus, which is why in QBE you fill values into columns.

**Safety.** The formula $\{\, t \mid \neg (t \in R) \,\}$ denotes every tuple in the universe that is not in $R$ — an infinite answer. A calculus expression is **safe** if every value in its result, and every value that the quantifiers range over, comes from the **domain of the formula** $\text{dom}(P)$: the finite set of constants appearing in $P$ together with all values appearing in the relations mentioned by $P$. Only safe expressions correspond to algebra expressions. Codd's equivalence is precisely: *relational algebra $\equiv$ safe TRC $\equiv$ safe DRC*.

Also worth knowing: relational algebra cannot express **transitive closure** (the ancestors of a node in a recursive `manager` relation) or **aggregation**. Both need extensions — SQL adds aggregates and `WITH RECURSIVE`, and Datalog adds recursion (topic 4.7).

blocks.title: Worked example — translating one English query three ways
blocks.text:
Schema: `EMP(eid, name, dept, sal)`, `DEPT(dept, dname, city)`.

Query: *names of employees who work in a department located in Mumbai and earn more than 60000.*

**Algebra.**
$$\pi_{name}\Big( \sigma_{sal > 60000 \,\wedge\, city = \text{'Mumbai'}} \big( \text{EMP} \bowtie \text{DEPT} \big) \Big)$$
Optimised form — push selections below the join so the join input is smaller:
$$\pi_{name}\Big( \sigma_{sal>60000}(\text{EMP}) \;\bowtie\; \pi_{dept}\big(\sigma_{city=\text{'Mumbai'}}(\text{DEPT})\big) \Big)$$
Both give the same relation; the second is what an optimiser produces.

**Tuple calculus.**
$$\{\, t \mid \exists e \in \text{EMP}\; \exists d \in \text{DEPT}\;( e.dept = d.dept \wedge d.city=\text{'Mumbai'} \wedge e.sal > 60000 \wedge t.name = e.name ) \,\}$$

**Domain calculus.**
$$\{\, \langle n \rangle \mid \exists i,p,s,q,c\; ( \langle i,n,p,s\rangle \in \text{EMP} \wedge \langle p,q,c\rangle \in \text{DEPT} \wedge c = \text{'Mumbai'} \wedge s > 60000 ) \,\}$$

Note how the shared variable $p$ in the DRC version *is* the join condition — equality is expressed by reusing a variable name rather than by writing an explicit predicate.

blocks.q: $R(A,B)$ has 200 tuples and $S(B,C)$ has 100 tuples. $B$ is the primary key of $S$ and a NOT NULL foreign key in $R$. How many tuples does $R \bowtie S$ have?
blocks.exp: Each tuple of $R$ carries a non-null $B$ value that must exist in $S$, and $S$ has exactly one tuple per $B$ value because $B$ is its key. So every $R$ tuple joins with exactly one $S$ tuple: the result has $|R| = 200$ tuples. The foreign-key-to-key case always gives exactly the child's cardinality.

blocks.q: Which of these is NOT a basic operator of relational algebra?
blocks.exp: The six basic operators are selection, projection, union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename. Natural join is derived: $R \bowtie S = \pi_{\text{all,\,one\,copy}}(\sigma_{\text{equality on common attrs}}(R \times S))$. Intersection, division, theta join and the outer joins are also derived.

blocks.q: $R(A,B,C,D)$ and $S(C,D)$. The degree and maximum cardinality of $R \div S$, given $|R| = 40$ and $|S| = 5$, are
blocks.exp: Degree of the quotient is $\deg(R) - \deg(S) = 4 - 2 = 2$, namely $(A,B)$. Each surviving $(A,B)$ pair needs all 5 tuples of $S$ present in $R$, so at most $\lfloor 40/5 \rfloor = 8$ distinct pairs can qualify.

tricks.title: Division = 'for all' = NOT EXISTS twice
tricks.body: Whenever a query says *every*, *all* or *without exception*, it is division. In algebra use $\pi_X(R) - \pi_X((\pi_X(R)\times S) - R)$; in calculus use $\forall$; in SQL use the double `NOT EXISTS`. Recognising the word is most of the work.

tricks.title: Degree arithmetic is free marks
tricks.body: $\deg(R\times S)=\deg R+\deg S$; $\deg(R\bowtie S)=\deg R+\deg S-|\text{common attrs}|$; $\deg(R\div S)=\deg R-\deg S$; $\deg(\sigma(R))=\deg R$; union/difference preserve degree. Many questions ask only for the degree.

tricks.title: Upper bound on division: $\lfloor |R|/|S| \rfloor$
tricks.body: Every qualifying $X$-value consumes $|S|$ tuples of $R$, so the quotient can never have more than $|R|/|S|$ tuples. This kills two options instantly in cardinality questions.

tricks.title: Push selections and projections down
tricks.body: $\sigma_c(R\bowtie S) = \sigma_c(R) \bowtie S$ when $c$ mentions only $R$'s attributes, and $\sigma_{c_1\wedge c_2} = \sigma_{c_1}\sigma_{c_2}$. Equivalence questions are answered by checking whether each condition's attributes really belong to the relation it was pushed into.

tricks.title: No shared attribute name $\Rightarrow$ natural join is a cross product
tricks.body: Examiners renames a column and asks for the result size. If the schemas share nothing, $|R \bowtie S| = |R|\cdot|S|$ and the degree is the sum of the degrees.

traps.title: Projection silently removes duplicates; SQL's SELECT does not
traps.body: $\pi_{dept}(\text{EMP})$ over 200 employees in 5 departments yields 5 tuples. `SELECT dept FROM emp` yields 200 rows. Any question comparing an algebra expression with a SQL statement is usually testing exactly this, and `DISTINCT` is the bridge.

traps.title: Equijoin keeps the join column twice, natural join keeps it once
traps.body: $\deg(R \bowtie_{R.B=S.B} S) = \deg R + \deg S$, but $\deg(R \bowtie S) = \deg R + \deg S - 1$. Degree questions turn on this one difference.

traps.title: Division needs *all* of $S$, not *only* $S$
traps.body: A tuple with extra associations still qualifies. Deepa taking AI as well as the three core courses is still in the answer. The opposite reading — 'exactly the set $S$' — is a different, harder query.

traps.title: Unsafe calculus expressions have no algebra equivalent
traps.body: $\{t \mid \neg(t \in R)\}$ is a legal formula but an infinite relation. Codd's equivalence is between algebra and *safe* calculus only, so an option stating that relational algebra is equivalent to full tuple calculus is false.

topics.title: SQL
topics.summary: Query evaluation order, every kind of join, nested and correlated subqueries, aggregates with GROUP BY and HAVING, views and updatability, triggers, and the many ways NULL breaks intuition.

blocks.text:
## The schema used throughout

Every example below runs against these two tables, which are also the ones in the lab on this page.

```
emp(eid, name, dept, sal, age, mgr)      -- mgr is the eid of the employee's manager, NULL for the boss
dept(dept, dname, city)                  -- dept is the primary key; emp.dept references it
```

## The logical order of evaluation

SQL is written in one order and evaluated in another. Knowing the evaluation order explains almost every "why is this an error" question.

$$\texttt{FROM} \to \texttt{WHERE} \to \texttt{GROUP BY} \to \texttt{HAVING} \to \texttt{SELECT} \to \texttt{DISTINCT} \to \texttt{ORDER BY} \to \texttt{LIMIT}$$

Three consequences follow immediately.

1. **`WHERE` cannot use an aggregate**, because grouping has not happened yet. Filtering on an aggregate is `HAVING`'s job.
2. **`WHERE` cannot use a `SELECT` alias** in standard SQL, because `SELECT` runs later. `ORDER BY` *can*, because it runs after `SELECT`.
3. **`HAVING` without `GROUP BY`** treats the whole table as one group and is legal: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;` returns a row only if there are more than five employees.

The conceptual evaluation of `FROM a, b` is the Cartesian product, then `WHERE` filters it. That is why a missing join condition produces $|a| \times |b|$ rows rather than an error.

## Joins, all of them

**Inner join.** Only matching rows.

```sql
SELECT e.name, d.city
FROM   emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.dept;
```

**Natural join** matches on *all* identically named columns automatically — here just `dept` — and keeps one copy:

```sql
SELECT name, city FROM emp NATURAL JOIN dept;
```

It is convenient and dangerous: add a column named `city` to `emp` later and the join condition silently changes.

**Left outer join.** Every `emp` row survives; unmatched ones get NULL for `dept`'s columns. Use it to *find* the unmatched rows:

```sql
SELECT e.name
FROM   emp e LEFT JOIN dept d ON e.dept = d.dept
WHERE  d.dept IS NULL;              -- employees in no known department
```

**Right outer join** is the mirror image; **full outer join** keeps unmatched rows from both sides. `CROSS JOIN` is the explicit Cartesian product.

**Self join.** Needed whenever a table is compared with itself. Employees paired with their managers:

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM   emp e JOIN emp m ON e.mgr = m.eid;
```

Note that this inner self-join *drops* the top boss, whose `mgr` is NULL. Changing `JOIN` to `LEFT JOIN` keeps that row with `manager` NULL — a classic two-option exam contrast.

**Set operators.** `UNION` removes duplicates, `UNION ALL` does not; `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` (called `MINUS` in Oracle) likewise default to removing duplicates. All require the same number of columns with compatible types. Cost note: `UNION` must sort or hash to deduplicate, so `UNION ALL` is strictly cheaper when you know the inputs are disjoint.
