blocks.text:
## Why the relational model needed extending

The plain relational model assumes atomic values, a single current state, one machine and a client that is always connected. Each of the models below relaxes exactly one of those assumptions, and exam questions almost always test *which* assumption was relaxed and *what new vocabulary* came with it.

## Temporal databases

A temporal database stores *when* a fact was true, not only that it is true now. Two independent time dimensions:

- **Valid time** — when the fact is true in the modelled world. An employee's salary was 50,000 from 2019-01-01 to 2021-03-31.
- **Transaction time** — when the fact was recorded in the database. Transaction time is append-only and cannot be changed retroactively, because it records what the system believed.

A relation with valid time only is a **historical** relation; with transaction time only, a **rollback** relation; with both, a **bitemporal** relation. Time is represented as **instants**, **intervals** $[t_s, t_e)$ or **time periods**, and the granularity (day, second) is called the **chronon**.

Temporal keys are the twist: a key like `eid` is no longer unique, because one employee has several rows with different validity intervals. The key becomes `eid` plus the valid-time start, with the constraint that intervals for one `eid` must not overlap — **temporal (sequenced) integrity**.

Operations get temporal variants: a **temporal join** matches tuples only where their time intervals **overlap**; **coalescing** merges value-equivalent adjacent intervals into one. SQL:2011 added `PERIOD FOR`, `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` and `FOR PORTION OF` for exactly these.

## Spatial and multimedia databases

**Spatial databases** store points, lines and regions with operators such as *contains*, *intersects*, *within distance* and *nearest neighbour*. B$^+$ trees are useless here because they order on one dimension, so spatial systems use **R-trees** (bounding rectangles arranged in a balanced tree), **quadtrees** (recursive subdivision into four), **k-d trees** and **grid files**.

**Multimedia databases** store images, audio and video. The retrieval problem is **content-based**: a query is "find images similar to this one", answered by extracting **feature vectors** (colour histograms, texture, shape descriptors, audio spectral features) and doing **nearest-neighbour search in high-dimensional space** under some distance metric. Because exact match is meaningless, results are **ranked by similarity** rather than being a set. Continuous media (audio, video) additionally need **isochronous delivery** — a guaranteed data rate — which ordinary DBMS buffering does not provide. The gap between low-level features and human meaning is the **semantic gap**.

## Active and deductive databases

An **active database** reacts to events by itself, using **ECA rules** (event–condition–action) — triggers, formalised. The design choices are the ones you already saw with triggers: *immediate* versus *deferred* (until commit) versus *detached* execution; *row-level* versus *statement-level* granularity; and conflict resolution when several rules fire, usually by priority. The dangers are **non-termination** (rules triggering each other in a cycle) and unpredictable interaction, so rule sets are analysed for **confluence** (same final state regardless of firing order) and **termination**.

A **deductive database** combines a set of **facts** (the extensional database, EDB — ordinary tables) with a set of **rules** (the intensional database, IDB) written in **Datalog**, a function-free subset of Prolog with set semantics and no ordering dependence.

A Datalog rule is $\text{head} \leftarrow \text{body}$, read right to left as an implication. Rules must be **safe**: every variable in the head must appear in a positive literal of the body, so the answer stays finite. Negation is allowed only in **stratified** form — a predicate may not depend negatively on itself, directly or through a cycle — which guarantees a unique intended model.

Datalog's decisive advantage over relational algebra is **recursion**: transitive closure is one rule.

blocks.title: Worked example — evaluating a recursive Datalog program
blocks.text:
EDB facts: `parent(a,b). parent(b,c). parent(c,d).`

IDB rules:
```
anc(X,Y) :- parent(X,Y).
anc(X,Y) :- parent(X,Z), anc(Z,Y).
```

**Naive bottom-up (fixpoint) evaluation.** Start with $\text{anc}_0 = \varnothing$ and apply both rules repeatedly until nothing new appears.

*Iteration 1.* Rule 1 contributes every parent fact:
$$\text{anc}_1 = \{(a,b),\,(b,c),\,(c,d)\}$$

*Iteration 2.* Rule 2 joins `parent` with $\text{anc}_1$ on the middle argument: $\text{parent}(a,b)$ with $\text{anc}(b,c)$ gives $(a,c)$; $\text{parent}(b,c)$ with $\text{anc}(c,d)$ gives $(b,d)$; $\text{parent}(c,d)$ has no $\text{anc}(d,\cdot)$.
$$\text{anc}_2 = \text{anc}_1 \cup \{(a,c),\,(b,d)\}$$

*Iteration 3.* $\text{parent}(a,b)$ with the new $\text{anc}(b,d)$ gives $(a,d)$; nothing else is new.
$$\text{anc}_3 = \text{anc}_2 \cup \{(a,d)\}$$

*Iteration 4.* No new tuple is derivable — **fixpoint reached**.

$$\text{anc} = \{(a,b),(b,c),(c,d),(a,c),(b,d),(a,d)\} \quad — \text{6 tuples}$$

which is exactly the transitive closure of a 3-edge chain, $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ ordered ancestor pairs. Note that naive evaluation recomputes $\text{anc}_1$ and $\text{anc}_2$ at every round; **semi-naive** evaluation joins only against the tuples *newly derived in the previous round*, which is why it is the algorithm actually used.

## XML and semi-structured data

Semi-structured data carries its own schema: each object describes its own attributes, so two objects of the "same kind" may differ. XML is the canonical example — a tree of **elements** with **attributes**, **text** content and a single root.

- **Well-formed** means syntactically correct: one root, properly nested, every tag closed, attribute values quoted.
- **Valid** means well-formed **and** conforming to a **DTD** or an **XML Schema (XSD)**.
- **DTD** can express element nesting and occurrence ($?$, $*$, $+$), ID/IDREF references, but has no data types and is not itself XML. **XSD** is written in XML, supports rich data types, namespaces, and user-defined types — which is the usual "difference between DTD and XSD" answer.

Querying: **XPath** navigates with path expressions (`/university/dept[@id='cs']/faculty/name`, with axes `child`, `descendant`, `parent`, `following-sibling` and predicates in `[ ]`); **XQuery** wraps XPath in the **FLWOR** expression — `for`, `let`, `where`, `order by`, `return`; **XSLT** transforms one document into another.

Storage options for XML in a DBMS: shred it into relations (fast queries, expensive reassembly), store it as a CLOB/BLOB with a text index (fast reassembly, slow queries), or use a **native XML** store. The corresponding modern format, JSON, gets the same treatment in document stores (topic 4.9).

## Mobile databases

A mobile client is intermittently connected, energy-limited and moves between cells. That breaks assumptions the classic architecture takes for granted.

- **Disconnection** is normal, not a failure, so clients keep a **local cached replica** and work offline, then **reconcile** on reconnection. Optimistic replication with conflict detection is the norm; strict two-phase locking across a wireless link is not viable.
- **Broadcast disks** push hot data over a broadcast channel so that many clients read without asking; access time then depends on where in the broadcast cycle the item sits.
- **Location-dependent queries** ("nearest fuel station") make the answer a function of the client's position, so the same query returns different results as the user moves; **location management** tracks users through **home location registers** and **visitor location registers**.
- Transactions are restructured: **Kangaroo transactions** hand off responsibility as a user moves between base stations, and long-lived work is split into compensatable **sagas** rather than held under locks.

## Distributed databases

A **distributed database** is a single logical database whose data is physically spread over several sites connected by a network, managed by a **DDBMS** that makes the distribution invisible. Contrast it with a **parallel database**, where multiple processors serve one tightly coupled machine (shared-memory, shared-disk or shared-nothing architectures).

**Homogeneous** DDBMS: same DBMS software at every site, cooperating fully. **Heterogeneous / federated / multidatabase**: different systems, each retaining **local autonomy**, integrated by a mediator — much harder, and the source of schema-integration problems (naming conflicts, scale conflicts, structural conflicts).

**Transparencies** the system should provide:

| Transparency | Hides |
|---|---|
| **Fragmentation** | that a relation is split into pieces |
| **Location (allocation)** | where each piece lives |
| **Replication** | that copies exist and which one was used |
| **Naming** | that sites use different local names |
| **Transaction / concurrency** | that a transaction touched several sites |
| **Failure** | that a site or link was down |

**Fragmentation**:

- **Horizontal** — split by rows using selection, $R_i = \sigma_{P_i}(R)$. Correctness requires **completeness** (every tuple is in some fragment), **reconstruction** ($R = \bigcup R_i$) and **disjointness**.
- **Vertical** — split by columns, $R_i = \pi_{A_i}(R)$, with the **primary key repeated in every fragment** so that reconstruction is a lossless join, $R = R_1 \bowtie R_2 \bowtie \cdots$.
- **Mixed / hybrid** — a horizontal fragmentation of vertical fragments or vice versa.
- **Derived horizontal** — fragment a child relation according to the fragmentation of its parent so that joins stay local.

**Replication** improves read availability and read performance at the cost of write cost and consistency maintenance. Full replication gives maximum availability and the worst update cost; no replication (pure partitioning) the opposite.

**Distributed query processing** adds **communication cost** to the usual I/O and CPU costs, and on a slow network it dominates. The **semijoin** is the standard optimisation: instead of shipping a whole relation to join it, ship only the join column of the smaller side, filter the larger side against it, and ship back only the tuples that can possibly match.

blocks.title: Worked example — semijoin versus shipping the whole relation
blocks.text:
Site 1 holds `EMP` with 10,000 tuples of 100 bytes each. Site 2 holds `DEPT` with 20 tuples of 50 bytes each. The join is `EMP ⋈ DEPT` on `dept`, a 4-byte attribute, and the answer is wanted at Site 2. Only 2,000 employees belong to one of those 20 departments.

**Strategy A — ship `EMP` to Site 2.**
$$10{,}000 \times 100 = 1{,}000{,}000 \text{ bytes.}$$

**Strategy B — ship `DEPT` to Site 1, join, ship the result back.**
Ship out $20 \times 50 = 1{,}000$ bytes; the join result is 2,000 tuples of $100 + 50 - 4 = 146$ bytes, so shipping it back costs $2{,}000 \times 146 = 292{,}000$ bytes. Total $= 293{,}000$ bytes.

**Strategy C — semijoin.**
1. At Site 2 compute $\pi_{\text{dept}}(\text{DEPT})$: 20 values of 4 bytes $= \mathbf{80}$ bytes. Ship to Site 1.
2. At Site 1 compute $\text{EMP} \ltimes \text{DEPT}$ — the 2,000 matching employee tuples — and ship them to Site 2: $2{,}000 \times 100 = \mathbf{200{,}000}$ bytes.
3. Site 2 completes the join locally at no communication cost.

Total $= 200{,}080$ bytes, about **five times cheaper than A** and cheaper than B.

The semijoin wins when the join column is small relative to a whole tuple **and** the selectivity is high (few tuples survive). If all 10,000 employees had matched, strategy C would cost $80 + 1{,}000{,}000$ bytes — *worse* than strategy A. That conditional benefit is the point examiners test.

## Distributed transactions and two-phase commit

A transaction touching several sites must commit everywhere or nowhere. The **two-phase commit protocol (2PC)** achieves this with a **coordinator** and **participants**.

**Phase 1 (voting / prepare).** The coordinator writes $\langle \text{prepare} \rangle$ to its log and sends `PREPARE` to every participant. Each participant either force-writes a `ready` record plus all its log records and replies `VOTE-COMMIT`, or replies `VOTE-ABORT`. After voting `ready`, a participant is **in doubt** — it may neither commit nor abort on its own, and it continues to hold its locks.

**Phase 2 (decision).** If *all* votes are commit, the coordinator force-writes $\langle \text{commit} \rangle$ and broadcasts `GLOBAL-COMMIT`; a single abort vote makes it broadcast `GLOBAL-ABORT`. Participants act and acknowledge.

The famous weakness is the **blocking problem**: if the coordinator crashes after collecting votes but before broadcasting the decision, every in-doubt participant is stuck holding locks until the coordinator recovers. **Three-phase commit (3PC)** inserts a *pre-commit* phase so that a surviving participant can infer the decision, making it non-blocking — but only if the network does not partition, which is why 2PC remains standard in practice.

Concurrency control across sites uses distributed 2PL (a **primary-copy** or **majority** protocol for replicas) or distributed timestamps built from (local counter, site id) pairs. Deadlock detection needs either a central detector or a distributed algorithm such as **edge chasing**, both complicated by **phantom deadlocks** — cycles that appear in a stale global wait-for graph but no longer exist.

blocks.q: For a vertical fragmentation of $R$ to be lossless, each fragment must contain
opts: all attributes appearing in some FD
blocks.exp: Vertical fragments are reconstructed by a natural join, and the binary lossless-join test requires the common attributes to be a superkey of a fragment. Repeating the primary key in every fragment guarantees this; without it the join produces spurious tuples.

blocks.q: In two-phase commit, a participant that has voted COMMIT and not yet heard the decision is
opts: free to commit locally after a timeout
free to abort locally after a timeout
in doubt and must hold its locks until it learns the decision
required to elect itself the new coordinator immediately
blocks.exp: Having voted to commit, the participant has surrendered its right to decide: the global outcome may still be abort if another participant voted no. It must keep its locks and wait, which is exactly the blocking problem that three-phase commit was invented to remove.

blocks.q: Which statement about Datalog is TRUE?
opts: Datalog rules may contain function symbols
Every variable in a rule head must also appear in a positive body literal
Negation may appear anywhere, including recursively
blocks.exp: That is the safety condition, and it is what keeps derived relations finite. Datalog is deliberately function-free, it expresses transitive closure in two rules, and negation is restricted to stratified programs so that no predicate depends negatively on itself.

tricks.title: Valid time is about the world, transaction time is about the database
tricks.body: Any temporal question reduces to which clock is meant. Retroactive corrections change valid time and add a new transaction-time version; transaction time itself is append-only and can never be edited. Both together = bitemporal.

tricks.title: Horizontal fragments use selection, vertical fragments use projection
tricks.body: So horizontal reconstructs by **union** and needs disjointness; vertical reconstructs by **join** and needs the key repeated. Naming the operator immediately gives you the correctness condition.

tricks.title: Semijoin pays off only when selectivity is high
tricks.body: Compare 'size of join column $\times$ number of distinct values' against 'saving on tuples that would not have matched'. If almost everything matches, shipping the whole relation is cheaper and the semijoin's extra round trip is wasted.

tricks.title: Count transparencies by what a user might otherwise have to write
tricks.body: If the user must name a site, location transparency is missing; if they must pick a copy, replication transparency; if they must assemble fragments, fragmentation transparency. The hierarchy is fragmentation $\supset$ location $\supset$ local mapping.

tricks.title: DTD versus XSD in one line each
tricks.body: DTD: not XML, no data types, has ID/IDREF, cardinality only via $?, *, +$. XSD: is XML, rich data types, namespaces, user-defined types, exact occurrence counts via `minOccurs`/`maxOccurs`.

traps.title: Distributed is not parallel
traps.body: A parallel database uses many processors on one tightly coupled system for speed; a distributed database spans autonomous sites over a network, primarily for locality, availability and organisational reasons. Shared-nothing is a parallel architecture, not a distribution model.

traps.title: Well-formed is not valid
traps.body: Every valid XML document is well-formed, but a document can be perfectly well-formed and violate its DTD. Validity is defined only relative to a schema; a document with no DTD can only be well-formed.

traps.title: 2PC is blocking; 3PC is non-blocking only without partitions
traps.body: Stating that three-phase commit removes blocking unconditionally is wrong: under a network partition it can still stall or, worse, diverge. The exam-safe statement is that 3PC is non-blocking under site failures with a reliable network.

traps.title: Replication helps reads and hurts writes
traps.body: Full replication maximises read availability and read performance while making every update a distributed transaction over all copies. Any option claiming replication improves update performance is wrong.

topics.title: Data Warehousing and Data Mining
topics.summary: OLTP versus OLAP, warehouse architecture and ETL, star and snowflake schemas, the data cube and its operations, and the mining algorithms — Apriori, decision trees, Bayes, SVM, KNN, clustering, HMM, link and sequence analysis.

blocks.text:
## Why a separate database for analysis

An operational database is tuned for many short transactions that touch a few rows each. An analyst's question — "compare quarterly sales of each product category across regions for the last three years" — scans millions of rows, joins a dozen tables and would cripple the operational system if run there. So the data is copied into a **data warehouse**: a **subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile** collection of data supporting decision making. Those four adjectives are Inmon's definition and are asked verbatim.

- **Subject-oriented** — organised around business subjects (sales, customer) rather than around applications.
- **Integrated** — inconsistent codes, units and names from many sources are reconciled to one standard.
- **Time-variant** — every record carries a time dimension; the warehouse keeps history rather than only the current state.
- **Non-volatile** — loaded and read, never updated transactionally; old values are not overwritten.

| | OLTP | OLAP |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | run the business | analyse the business |
| Data | current, detailed | historical, summarised |
| Unit of work | short read/write transaction | long read-only query |
| Access | tens of rows | millions of rows |
| Design | normalised (3NF), minimise redundancy | denormalised (star), minimise joins |
| Users | clerks, applications | analysts, managers |
| Metric | transactions per second | query response time |

**Architecture**: source systems $\to$ **ETL** (extract, transform, load; with a **staging area** for cleaning, deduplication and conformance) $\to$ warehouse plus **data marts** (departmental subsets) $\to$ OLAP servers $\to$ query, reporting and mining tools, all described by a **metadata repository**. A **data mart** can be *dependent* (fed from the warehouse) or *independent* (fed directly from sources — faster to build, but it re-creates the integration problem). An **operational data store** sits between OLTP and the warehouse, holding current integrated data for operational reporting. **ELT** reverses the last two steps so that transformation happens inside a powerful target engine.

## Multidimensional modelling: star, snowflake, constellation

The warehouse is modelled as **facts** measured along **dimensions**.

A **fact table** holds the numeric **measures** (`units_sold`, `revenue`) plus foreign keys to the dimension tables. Its primary key is the combination of those foreign keys, so it is long and narrow and holds almost all the rows. Measures are classified as **additive** (summable across every dimension, e.g. revenue), **semi-additive** (summable across some, e.g. an inventory level — not over time) and **non-additive** (a ratio or percentage).

A **dimension table** holds the descriptive attributes (`product_name`, `category`, `brand`) and is short and wide.

- **Star schema** — one fact table surrounded by **denormalised** dimension tables, one table per dimension. Fewer joins, faster queries, some redundancy in dimensions.
- **Snowflake schema** — the dimension tables are **normalised** into hierarchies (`product $\to$ category $\to$ department` as three tables). Less storage, easier dimension maintenance, but more joins and slower queries.
- **Fact constellation (galaxy)** — several fact tables sharing **conformed dimensions**, for example `sales` and `shipments` both using the same `time` and `product` dimensions.

Star versus snowflake is the most asked pair in this topic: *star is denormalised and fast; snowflake is normalised and compact*. A snowflake of depth 1 is a star.

**Slowly changing dimensions** describe what to do when a dimension attribute changes: **Type 1** overwrite (history lost), **Type 2** add a new row with a surrogate key and validity dates (history kept — the usual choice), **Type 3** add a "previous value" column (one step of history).

## The data cube and OLAP operations

A **data cube** presents a fact table as an $n$-dimensional array of aggregates. The **cuboid lattice** for $n$ dimensions contains $2^n$ cuboids, from the **base cuboid** (all dimensions, finest grain) to the **apex cuboid** (no dimension, a single grand total). If dimension $i$ has a hierarchy with $L_i$ levels (counting the "all" level), the number of cuboids is $\prod_{i=1}^{n}(L_i + 1)$.

The five operations:

| Operation | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Roll-up** | aggregate by climbing a hierarchy (city $\to$ state $\to$ country) or by dropping a dimension — result is coarser |
| **Drill-down** | the reverse: descend a hierarchy or add a dimension — result is finer |
| **Slice** | fix **one** dimension to one value, producing a sub-cube of dimension $n-1$ |
| **Dice** | restrict **two or more** dimensions to ranges of values, producing a sub-cube of the same dimensionality |
| **Pivot (rotate)** | re-orient the axes for presentation; no change to the data |

Also **drill-across** (combine two fact tables on conformed dimensions) and **drill-through** (jump from the summary down to the underlying operational rows).

Implementation servers:

- **ROLAP** — data stays in relational tables; cubes are SQL with `GROUP BY`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP` and `GROUPING SETS`. Scales to huge volumes, slower per query.
- **MOLAP** — data stored in a proprietary multidimensional array; very fast, but suffers from **sparsity** (most cells empty) and does not scale as far.
- **HOLAP** — detail in relational storage, aggregates in multidimensional storage.

Because full pre-aggregation is exponential, systems pre-compute a **selected subset** of cuboids — the materialised-view selection problem — and answer the rest from them.

## Knowledge discovery and the mining tasks

**KDD** is the whole pipeline; **data mining** is one step inside it: *selection $\to$ preprocessing (cleaning, missing values, noise) $\to$ transformation (normalisation, discretisation, reduction) $\to$ **mining** $\to$ pattern evaluation $\to$ knowledge presentation*. Roughly 70–80% of effort is preprocessing.

Tasks split into **descriptive** (association, clustering, summarisation, outlier detection) and **predictive** (classification, regression, sequence prediction). Classification is **supervised** — labelled training data; clustering is **unsupervised**.

## Association rule mining and Apriori

For an itemset $X$ in a transaction database $D$:

$$\text{support}(X) = \frac{|\{t \in D : X \subseteq t\}|}{|D|}, \qquad \text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{support}(X \cup Y)}{\text{support}(X)}$$

$$\text{lift}(X \Rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{confidence}(X \Rightarrow Y)}{\text{support}(Y)}$$

Lift $> 1$ means positive correlation, $= 1$ independence, $< 1$ negative correlation. Confidence alone is misleading — a rule can have 80% confidence while $Y$ appears in 90% of all transactions, so lift $< 1$ and the rule is worse than guessing.

**Apriori** rests on the **downward-closure (anti-monotone) property**: *every subset of a frequent itemset is frequent*, equivalently *every superset of an infrequent itemset is infrequent*. So candidates of size $k$ are formed by self-joining $L_{k-1}$ on their first $k-2$ items, then **pruned** by checking that all $k$ of their $(k-1)$-subsets are in $L_{k-1}$, then counted in one database pass.

Apriori needs up to $k_{\max}+1$ database scans and can generate huge candidate sets. **FP-growth** avoids candidate generation entirely by building an **FP-tree** in **two scans** and mining it recursively with conditional pattern bases — the usual "improvement over Apriori" answer.

blocks.title: Worked example — full Apriori trace
blocks.text:
$D$ with 5 transactions, minimum support count 2 (40%).

| TID | Items |
|---|---|
| T1 | A, C, D |
| T2 | B, C, E |
| T3 | A, B, C, E |
| T4 | B, E |
| T5 | A, B, C, E |

**Pass 1.** Counts: $A=3$ (T1,T3,T5), $B=4$ (T2–T5), $C=4$ (T1,T2,T3,T5), $D=1$ (T1), $E=4$ (T2–T5).
$D$ fails ($1 < 2$) and is dropped. $L_1 = \{A{:}3,\ B{:}4,\ C{:}4,\ E{:}4\}$.

**Pass 2.** $C_2$ = all pairs from $L_1$: $AB, AC, AE, BC, BE, CE$. Note no pair containing $D$ is even considered — that is the pruning at work.
Counts: $AB=2$ (T3,T5); $AC=3$ (T1,T3,T5); $AE=2$ (T3,T5); $BC=3$ (T2,T3,T5); $BE=4$ (T2,T3,T4,T5); $CE=3$ (T2,T3,T5).
All six pass. $L_2 = \{AB{:}2, AC{:}3, AE{:}2, BC{:}3, BE{:}4, CE{:}3\}$.

**Pass 3.** Self-join $L_2$ on the shared first item: $AB \bowtie AC \to ABC$; $AB \bowtie AE \to ABE$; $AC \bowtie AE \to ACE$; $BC \bowtie BE \to BCE$. Candidate set $\{ABC, ABE, ACE, BCE\}$.
Prune: $ABC$ needs $AB, AC, BC$ — all in $L_2$, keep. $ABE$ needs $AB, AE, BE$ — keep. $ACE$ needs $AC, AE, CE$ — keep. $BCE$ needs $BC, BE, CE$ — keep. Nothing pruned this round.
Counts: $ABC=2$ (T3,T5); $ABE=2$ (T3,T5); $ACE=2$ (T3,T5); $BCE=3$ (T2,T3,T5).
$L_3 = \{ABC{:}2, ABE{:}2, ACE{:}2, BCE{:}3\}$.

**Pass 4.** Join $ABC \bowtie ABE \to ABCE$. Prune: its 3-subsets are $ABC, ABE, ACE, BCE$ — all in $L_3$, so keep. Count $ABCE = 2$ (T3, T5). $L_4 = \{ABCE{:}2\}$.

**Pass 5.** Only one itemset in $L_4$, so no join is possible. $C_5 = \varnothing$ and the algorithm stops.

**Totals.** Frequent itemsets: $4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = \mathbf{15}$. The single **maximal** frequent itemset is $ABCE$ (no frequent superset). **Closed** itemsets are those with no superset of equal support — for instance $AC$ (support 3) is closed since $ABC$, $ACE$ have support 2.

**Rules from $BCE$ (support 3, i.e. 0.6).**
- $BC \Rightarrow E$: confidence $= 3/3 = 100\%$; lift $= 1.0 / 0.8 = \mathbf{1.25}$ — genuinely informative.
- $E \Rightarrow BC$: confidence $= 3/4 = 75\%$; lift $= 0.75/0.6 = 1.25$ (lift is symmetric).
- $B \Rightarrow E$: confidence $= 4/4 = 100\%$; lift $= 1.0/0.8 = 1.25$.
- $A \Rightarrow BCE$: confidence $= 2/3 \approx 66.7\%$; lift $= 0.667/0.6 \approx 1.11$.

With a minimum confidence of 80%, $A \Rightarrow BCE$ and $E \Rightarrow BC$ are rejected while $BC \Rightarrow E$ and $B \Rightarrow E$ survive.

## Classification

**Decision trees** split the data recursively on the attribute that best separates the classes. Splitting criteria:

$$\text{Entropy}(S) = -\sum_{i} p_i \log_2 p_i, \qquad \text{Gain}(S,A) = \text{Entropy}(S) - \sum_{v \in A} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\,\text{Entropy}(S_v)$$

$$\text{Gini}(S) = 1 - \sum_i p_i^2$$

**ID3** uses information gain and is biased towards attributes with many values; **C4.5** corrects this with the **gain ratio** (gain divided by the split information) and handles continuous attributes and missing values; **CART** uses the Gini index and builds strictly binary trees. Overfitting is controlled by **pre-pruning** (stop early) or **post-pruning** (grow fully, then cut back using a validation set).

**Naive Bayes** applies $P(C \mid X) \propto P(C)\prod_j P(x_j \mid C)$ under the (usually false but useful) assumption that attributes are conditionally independent given the class. Zero counts are fixed by **Laplace smoothing**.

**$k$-nearest neighbour** is a **lazy, instance-based** learner: no model is built at training time; classification computes the distance from the query point to every training point and takes a majority vote among the $k$ closest. Small $k$ means high variance and sensitivity to noise; large $k$ oversmooths. Attributes must be normalised, or the attribute with the largest range dominates the distance.

**Support vector machines** find the hyperplane $w^{T}x + b = 0$ that **maximises the margin** between classes. Only the training points lying on the margin — the **support vectors** — determine the solution; the margin width is $2/\lVert w \rVert$, so maximising the margin means minimising $\lVert w \rVert^2/2$. Non-separable data is handled by **slack variables** with a penalty $C$ (soft margin) and non-linear boundaries by the **kernel trick**: replace the dot product with $K(x_i,x_j)$ — polynomial, RBF/Gaussian, sigmoid — so the data is implicitly mapped into a higher-dimensional space where it is separable, without ever computing that mapping.

**Evaluation.** From the confusion matrix: $\text{accuracy} = \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}$, $\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}$, $\text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}$, and $F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P+R}$. Use $k$-fold cross-validation, and prefer precision/recall to accuracy on imbalanced data.

blocks.title: Worked example — information gain for a decision-tree split
blocks.text:
A training set $S$ of 14 days with class `Play` $\in \{$yes, no$\}$: 9 yes, 5 no.

**Entropy of the whole set.**
$$\text{Entropy}(S) = -\frac{9}{14}\log_2\frac{9}{14} - \frac{5}{14}\log_2\frac{5}{14}$$
$\frac{9}{14} = 0.643$ and $\log_2 0.643 = -0.637$, so the first term is $0.643 \times 0.637 = 0.410$.
$\frac{5}{14} = 0.357$ and $\log_2 0.357 = -1.486$, so the second term is $0.357 \times 1.486 = 0.530$.
$$\text{Entropy}(S) = 0.410 + 0.530 = \mathbf{0.940}$$

**Split on `Outlook`**, which partitions the 14 days into Sunny (5 days: 2 yes, 3 no), Overcast (4 days: 4 yes, 0 no) and Rain (5 days: 3 yes, 2 no).

- $\text{Entropy}(\text{Sunny}) = -\frac{2}{5}\log_2\frac{2}{5} - \frac{3}{5}\log_2\frac{3}{5} = 0.4(1.322) + 0.6(0.737) = 0.529 + 0.442 = 0.971$
- $\text{Entropy}(\text{Overcast}) = 0$ — pure node, all yes.
- $\text{Entropy}(\text{Rain}) = 0.971$ by the same 3/2 split.

**Weighted entropy after the split:**
$$\frac{5}{14}(0.971) + \frac{4}{14}(0) + \frac{5}{14}(0.971) = 0.347 + 0 + 0.347 = 0.694$$

$$\text{Gain}(S, \text{Outlook}) = 0.940 - 0.694 = \mathbf{0.246}$$

If the competing attributes give $\text{Gain}(\text{Humidity}) = 0.151$, $\text{Gain}(\text{Wind}) = 0.048$ and $\text{Gain}(\text{Temperature}) = 0.029$, then `Outlook` has the highest gain and becomes the root. The Overcast branch is already pure and becomes a leaf labelled *yes*; the Sunny and Rain branches are split recursively.

**Gini for comparison:** $\text{Gini}(S) = 1 - (9/14)^2 - (5/14)^2 = 1 - 0.413 - 0.128 = 0.459$. Gini and entropy almost always choose the same attribute; Gini is cheaper because it avoids logarithms.

## Clustering, HMMs, link and sequence analysis

**Clustering** groups unlabelled objects so that intra-cluster similarity is high and inter-cluster similarity low.

- **$k$-means** (partitioning): choose $k$ centroids, assign each point to the nearest, recompute centroids as means, repeat until stable. Cost $O(nkt)$ per run. It needs $k$ in advance, is sensitive to the initial seeds and to outliers, and finds only spherical, similarly sized clusters. **$k$-medoids (PAM)** uses actual data points as centres and is more robust to outliers but costlier.
- **Hierarchical**: **agglomerative** (bottom-up, merge the closest pair) or **divisive** (top-down), visualised as a **dendrogram** that you cut at a chosen height. Linkage choices — single (nearest pair, produces chaining), complete (farthest pair, compact clusters), average, centroid — change the result substantially. Cost is at least $O(n^2)$, and merges cannot be undone.
- **Density-based (DBSCAN)**: parameters $\varepsilon$ and `MinPts`; a **core point** has at least `MinPts` neighbours within $\varepsilon$; clusters grow by density-reachability. It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, needs no $k$, and labels low-density points as **noise** — its distinguishing advantage over $k$-means.
- **Grid-based** (STING, CLIQUE) and **model-based** (EM with Gaussian mixtures) round out the standard taxonomy.

**Hidden Markov models** describe a system that moves through **hidden states** by a Markov transition matrix $A$ while emitting **observable symbols** by an emission matrix $B$, starting from distribution $\pi$. Three canonical problems and their algorithms:

| Problem | Question | Algorithm |
|---|---|---|
| **Evaluation** | $P(O \mid \lambda)$ — how likely is this observation sequence? | **Forward** (or backward) algorithm, $O(N^2T)$ |
| **Decoding** | which hidden state sequence best explains $O$? | **Viterbi**, $O(N^2T)$, dynamic programming keeping the max instead of the sum |
| **Learning** | fit $A, B, \pi$ to data | **Baum–Welch** (an instance of EM) |

HMMs are used for speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging and biological sequence analysis.

**Link analysis** mines the graph structure of linked objects. **PageRank** models a random surfer: $PR(p) = \frac{1-d}{N} + d\sum_{q \to p} \frac{PR(q)}{L(q)}$ with damping factor $d \approx 0.85$ and $L(q)$ the out-degree of $q$; it is a query-independent, global score computed by power iteration. **HITS** instead computes, per query, two scores — **authority** (pointed to by good hubs) and **hub** (points to good authorities) — that reinforce each other. Related tasks are link prediction, community detection and centrality measures.

**Sequence analysis** mines ordered data. **Sequential pattern mining** (GSP, SPADE, PrefixSpan) finds subsequences frequent across many customer sequences — note that unlike association rules, *order matters and items may be separated by other items*. Time-series mining adds similarity search under Euclidean or **dynamic time warping** distance, trend and periodicity detection, and forecasting.

blocks.q: In a warehouse, aggregating sales from 'city' to 'state' is which OLAP operation?
blocks.exp: Climbing a concept hierarchy to a coarser level of aggregation is roll-up; the reverse is drill-down. Slice fixes one dimension to a single value, dice restricts two or more dimensions to subsets, and pivot only re-orients the presentation.

blocks.q: An itemset $\{A,B\}$ has support count 3 in a database where $\{A\}$ has count 3, $\{B\}$ has count 8 and $|D| = 10$. The confidence and lift of $A \Rightarrow B$ are
blocks.exp: Confidence $=\text{sup}(AB)/\text{sup}(A) = 3/3 = 100\%$. Lift $=$ confidence $/\,\text{sup}(B) = 1.0 / (8/10) = 1.25 > 1$, so $A$ and $B$ are positively correlated. Note the reverse rule $B \Rightarrow A$ would have confidence only $3/8 = 37.5\%$ — confidence is asymmetric, lift is not.

blocks.q: Which pair of statements correctly contrasts star and snowflake schemas?
opts: Star normalises dimensions; snowflake denormalises them
Star denormalises dimensions and needs fewer joins; snowflake normalises them and saves space
Both normalise the fact table; only snowflake normalises dimensions
Star supports multiple fact tables; snowflake supports only one
blocks.exp: In a star each dimension is a single denormalised table, so a query joins the fact table to one table per dimension. Snowflaking splits dimension hierarchies into normalised tables, reducing redundancy and storage at the cost of extra joins and slower queries. Multiple fact tables sharing dimensions is a fact constellation, not a distinguishing feature of either.

blocks.q: Which clustering algorithm does NOT require the number of clusters as an input and can label points as noise?
opts: Agglomerative hierarchical with a fixed cut
blocks.exp: DBSCAN is parameterised by $\varepsilon$ and MinPts, not by $k$; it derives the number of clusters from the density structure and explicitly marks low-density points as noise. Both $k$-means and $k$-medoids take $k$ as input, and cutting a dendrogram at a fixed height is equivalent to choosing the cluster count.

tricks.title: Apriori pruning: check every $(k-1)$-subset
tricks.body: A $k$-candidate survives only if **all** $k$ of its immediate subsets are frequent. Counting subsets is faster than counting transactions, so do the prune before touching the database — and in exam questions the pruned candidates are exactly what you are asked to name.

tricks.title: Confidence is asymmetric, lift is symmetric
tricks.body: $\text{lift}(X\Rightarrow Y) = \frac{\text{sup}(XY)}{\text{sup}(X)\text{sup}(Y)} = \text{lift}(Y \Rightarrow X)$, but the two confidences differ. If a question gives both directions with the same lift and different confidence, that is consistent, not a contradiction.

tricks.title: Count cuboids as $2^n$, or $\prod (L_i+1)$ with hierarchies
tricks.body: Without hierarchies, an $n$-dimensional cube has $2^n$ cuboids because each dimension is either present or aggregated away. With $L_i$ levels in dimension $i$, each dimension contributes $L_i+1$ choices (its levels plus 'all').

tricks.title: Entropy of a 50/50 split is exactly 1; of a pure node exactly 0
tricks.body: Use these anchors to sanity-check arithmetic. Any weighted child entropy must lie between 0 and the parent's entropy, so a 'gain' larger than the parent entropy or a negative gain means an arithmetic slip.

tricks.title: Match the algorithm to the word in the stem
tricks.body: *Maximum margin / support vectors / kernel* $\Rightarrow$ SVM. *Lazy / instance-based / no training phase* $\Rightarrow$ KNN. *Hidden states / Viterbi / emission* $\Rightarrow$ HMM. *Hubs and authorities* $\Rightarrow$ HITS; *random surfer / damping factor* $\Rightarrow$ PageRank. *Downward closure* $\Rightarrow$ Apriori. One keyword usually settles the option.

traps.title: High confidence does not mean a useful rule
traps.body: If $Y$ occurs in 90% of transactions, a rule with 80% confidence has lift $0.8/0.9 < 1$ and is worse than predicting $Y$ blindly. Any question offering confidence alone as the measure of 'interestingness' is testing this.

traps.title: Snowflake saves space, not time
traps.body: Normalising dimensions reduces redundancy but adds joins to every query. Since dimension tables are tiny compared with the fact table, the space saved is usually negligible and the extra joins are not — which is why real warehouses prefer stars.

traps.title: Classification is supervised, clustering is not
traps.body: Any option describing clustering as needing labelled data, or classification as discovering the classes, has them swapped. Association rule mining is also unsupervised and finds no classes at all.

traps.title: Apriori's property is about subsets, not supersets
traps.body: 'All subsets of a frequent itemset are frequent' is the correct statement; 'all supersets of a frequent itemset are frequent' is false. The contrapositive — any superset of an infrequent set is infrequent — is what does the pruning.

traps.title: A data warehouse is non-volatile, not read-only forever
traps.body: Non-volatility means the warehouse is not updated by operational transactions; it is still periodically **loaded** with new data and refreshed. Options saying a warehouse is never written to are wrong, as are options calling it a real-time copy of the OLTP database.

topics.title: Big Data and NOSQL
topics.summary: The Vs of big data, HDFS and its block/replica arithmetic, the MapReduce execution model, Spark, the four NOSQL families, and CAP, BASE and quorum consistency.

blocks.text:
## What makes data "big"

Big data is not a size threshold; it is the point at which the data's **volume, velocity or variety** defeats the tools you would normally reach for. The canonical list:

- **Volume** — petabytes, too much for one machine's disks.
- **Velocity** — data arriving as a continuous stream that must be processed as it lands.
- **Variety** — structured rows, semi-structured JSON and logs, unstructured text, image and video together.
- **Veracity** — uncertainty, noise and inconsistency in the data.
- **Value** — the point of the exercise; without it the other four are cost.
- *(Sometimes added)* **Variability** — the meaning and the load both change over time.

The structural response is **scale out, not up**: instead of a bigger server (vertical scaling, which hits a hard ceiling and a steep price curve), use many commodity machines (horizontal scaling). That decision forces everything else — data must be partitioned across machines, computation must be moved to the data rather than the data to the computation, and **failure of individual nodes must be treated as routine**, not exceptional.

## HDFS

The **Hadoop Distributed File System** stores very large files across a cluster with these design commitments: write-once-read-many access, streaming reads rather than low-latency random reads, very large blocks, and replication for fault tolerance.

- **NameNode** (master) holds the **namespace** and the block-to-DataNode map **in memory**, persisted as the `fsimage` file plus an `edits` journal. It stores **metadata only** — no file data ever passes through it. It is the single point of failure in Hadoop 1; Hadoop 2 adds a **standby NameNode** with automatic failover (the **Secondary NameNode** is *not* a standby — it only periodically merges `edits` into `fsimage`).
- **DataNodes** (workers) store the actual blocks and send **heartbeats** and **block reports**. A missing heartbeat triggers re-replication of that node's blocks elsewhere.
- **Block size** defaults to 128 MB (64 MB in older versions) — enormous compared with a 4 KB filesystem block. The reason is to make the seek time negligible relative to the transfer time, and to keep the NameNode's in-memory metadata small.
- **Replication factor** defaults to 3. The default **rack-aware placement** puts replica 1 on the local node, replica 2 on a node in a *different* rack, and replica 3 on another node in *that same* second rack — one cross-rack write, but survival of a whole rack failure.
- A file smaller than a block **does not waste** a whole block on disk: the last block occupies only what it needs. But every file, however small, costs the NameNode roughly 150 bytes of memory, which is why HDFS is bad at millions of small files — the **small files problem**.

**YARN** separates cluster resource management from the programming model: a global **ResourceManager**, a per-node **NodeManager**, and a per-job **ApplicationMaster** that negotiates **containers**. This is the main Hadoop 1 to Hadoop 2 change and lets Spark, Tez and MapReduce share one cluster.

## MapReduce

MapReduce is a programming model for embarrassingly parallel batch computation over a distributed file system. The user writes two functions:

$$\texttt{map}: (k_1, v_1) \longrightarrow \text{list}(k_2, v_2)$$
$$\texttt{reduce}: (k_2, \text{list}(v_2)) \longrightarrow \text{list}(k_3, v_3)$$

The framework supplies everything else: splitting the input, scheduling tasks near their data (**data locality**), the **shuffle and sort** that groups all values of a key onto one reducer, re-execution of failed tasks, and **speculative execution** of stragglers.

The full pipeline is **input split $\to$ map $\to$ [combine] $\to$ partition $\to$ shuffle and sort $\to$ reduce $\to$ output**.

- One **map task per input split**, and a split defaults to one HDFS block — so the number of mappers is determined by the input size, not by the programmer.
- The number of **reducers is set by the programmer**; the **partitioner** (by default `hash(key) mod numReducers`) decides which reducer gets which key.
- A **combiner** is a local, optional mini-reduce that runs on the map output to cut shuffle traffic. It may only be used when the reduce function is **commutative and associative** — sum, max, count work; **average does not**, which is the standard trap.
- The **shuffle** is the expensive phase, because it is all-to-all network traffic.

MapReduce's weakness is that every job writes its output to HDFS, so an iterative algorithm (k-means, PageRank, gradient descent) pays disk I/O every round. **Apache Spark** fixes this with **RDDs** — immutable, partitioned collections held in memory, whose **lineage** allows lost partitions to be recomputed rather than replicated. Spark distinguishes **transformations** (`map`, `filter`, `join` — lazy, they only build a DAG) from **actions** (`count`, `collect`, `saveAsTextFile` — these trigger execution). For iterative and interactive workloads Spark is typically an order of magnitude faster.

The surrounding ecosystem in one line each: **Hive** — SQL over Hadoop, compiled to MapReduce/Tez jobs; **Pig** — a dataflow scripting language; **HBase** — a wide-column store *on top of* HDFS giving random read/write; **Sqoop** — bulk transfer between RDBMS and HDFS; **Flume/Kafka** — streaming ingestion; **ZooKeeper** — distributed coordination and leader election; **Oozie** — workflow scheduling.

blocks.title: Worked example — HDFS arithmetic and a MapReduce word count
blocks.text:
**Part 1 — storage.** A 1 GB log file is stored in HDFS with a 128 MB block size and replication factor 3.

- Blocks: $\lceil 1024 / 128 \rceil = \mathbf{8}$ blocks.
- Block replicas across the cluster: $8 \times 3 = \mathbf{24}$.
- Raw disk consumed: $1\text{ GB} \times 3 = \mathbf{3}$ GB.
- Map tasks in a job reading this file with the default split size: **8**, one per block.

Now the same file is 1.25 GB. Blocks $= \lceil 1280/128 \rceil = 10$, of which the last is full; if the file were 1.26 GB the last block would hold only 10 MB but would still be *one* block — and it occupies 10 MB of disk, not 128 MB.

**Part 2 — word count.** Input split 1 contains `the cat sat`, split 2 contains `the cat ran`. Two mappers, two reducers, default hash partitioner.

*Map phase.* Mapper 1 emits $(\texttt{the},1), (\texttt{cat},1), (\texttt{sat},1)$. Mapper 2 emits $(\texttt{the},1), (\texttt{cat},1), (\texttt{ran},1)$.

*Combine phase (optional).* Nothing to combine here — every key appears once per mapper. Had split 1 been `the cat the`, the combiner would turn $(\texttt{the},1),(\texttt{the},1)$ into $(\texttt{the},2)$ before the shuffle, halving the bytes sent for that key.

*Partition and shuffle.* Say `hash` sends `the` and `ran` to reducer 0 and `cat` and `sat` to reducer 1. Reducer 0 receives $(\texttt{ran}, [1])$ and $(\texttt{the}, [1,1])$; reducer 1 receives $(\texttt{cat}, [1,1])$ and $(\texttt{sat}, [1])$. Note that the values for one key are guaranteed to arrive at exactly one reducer, and that keys arrive **sorted** within each reducer.

*Reduce phase.* Reducer 0 outputs $(\texttt{ran},1), (\texttt{the},2)$; reducer 1 outputs $(\texttt{cat},2), (\texttt{sat},1)$. Two output files are produced, one per reducer — the results are *not* merged into one globally sorted file unless a single reducer or a total-order partitioner is used.

**Part 3 — why average breaks a combiner.** Suppose the reduce function computes the mean. Mapper 1 emits values $2, 4$ for key $k$ and mapper 2 emits $9$. Correct answer: $(2+4+9)/3 = 5$. With a combiner that averages, mapper 1 sends $3$ and mapper 2 sends $9$, and the reducer computes $(3+9)/2 = 6$ — **wrong**. Averaging is not associative. The fix is to emit (sum, count) pairs and divide only in the reducer.

## The NOSQL families

"NOSQL" means *not only SQL*. These systems give up some of the relational package — a fixed schema, joins, full ACID — in exchange for horizontal scalability and flexible data shapes. Four families:

| Family | Data model | Query style | Typical systems |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Key–value** | opaque value under a unique key | get / put / delete by key only | Redis, Riak, DynamoDB, Memcached |
| **Document** | self-describing JSON/BSON/XML document per key | query on any field inside the document; secondary indexes | MongoDB, CouchDB |
| **Column-family (wide-column)** | rows with column families; each row may have different columns | key and column-range access; good for sparse data | Cassandra, HBase, BigTable |
| **Graph** | nodes and edges with properties | traversals, shortest path, pattern matching | Neo4j, JanusGraph |

The distinguishing points examiners use: a **key–value** store cannot query *inside* the value, while a **document** store can — that is the whole difference between the first two families. A **column-family** store is not a column-oriented relational database; it groups related columns into families stored together and is designed for very wide, very sparse rows. A **graph** database is the odd one out on scalability — relationships are stored as direct pointers, which makes traversal fast but makes partitioning across machines hard.

Most NOSQL systems are **schema-less** or schema-on-read (the application interprets the record) rather than schema-on-write, denormalise aggressively (store the order and its line items in one document rather than joining), and replicate by **sharding** on a partition key with **consistent hashing** so that adding a node moves only $1/n$ of the keys.

blocks.title: CAP, BASE and PACELC
blocks.text:
**CAP theorem (Brewer, proved by Gilbert and Lynch).** A distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee all three of:

- **Consistency** — every read sees the most recent write (this is *linearizability*, **not** the C of ACID).
- **Availability** — every non-failing node returns a response for every request.
- **Partition tolerance** — the system keeps working despite arbitrary message loss between nodes.

Since network partitions **will** happen in any real distributed system, $P$ is not optional. The theorem therefore really says: *during a partition, choose C or A*.

- **CP** — refuse requests on the minority side rather than serve stale data: HBase, MongoDB (default), ZooKeeper, Redis Cluster.
- **AP** — answer anyway and reconcile later: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, Riak.
- **CA** — only a single-site (non-distributed) system, so a traditional RDBMS. It is not a design option for a distributed store.

**BASE** is the AP-side philosophy that contrasts with ACID: **Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent** — if no new updates are made, all replicas eventually converge.

**PACELC** extends CAP with the case where there is no partition: *if **P**artition then **A** or **C**, **E**lse **L**atency or **C**onsistency*. It captures the fact that even a healthy system trades consistency against latency.

## Tunable consistency and quorums

Dynamo-style systems let the application choose consistency per operation. With $N$ replicas, $W$ the number of replicas that must acknowledge a write, and $R$ the number consulted on a read:

$$R + W > N \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{the read set and the write set overlap} \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{strong (read-your-writes) consistency}$$

$$W > N/2 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{no two writes can succeed concurrently on disjoint majorities}$$

Common settings with $N = 3$: $W = 1, R = 1$ gives lowest latency and only eventual consistency ($1+1 \not> 3$); $W = 3, R = 1$ gives fast reads and slow, fragile writes; $W = 2, R = 2$ is the usual balanced quorum since $2 + 2 > 3$.

Conflict resolution when two replicas diverge uses **vector clocks** (detect concurrent versions and hand both to the application), **last-write-wins** timestamps (simple, silently loses data), or **CRDTs** (data types designed so merges always converge). Repair mechanisms include **read repair**, **hinted handoff** and background **anti-entropy** with **Merkle trees**.

**NewSQL** systems (Spanner, CockroachDB, VoltDB) are the counter-movement: horizontal scalability *and* ACID transactions with SQL, typically by combining sharding with consensus protocols (Paxos or Raft) per shard, accepting extra latency in exchange for strong consistency.

blocks.q: A 500 MB file is stored in HDFS with 128 MB blocks and replication factor 3. How many blocks are created and how much raw disk is used?
blocks.exp: $\lceil 500/128 \rceil = 4$ blocks — three full 128 MB blocks and one holding the remaining 116 MB. Replication triples the space actually occupied, $500 \times 3 = 1500$ MB, because the partial last block consumes only its real size, not a full block.

blocks.q: In a quorum-replicated store with $N = 5$ replicas, which $(W, R)$ pair does NOT guarantee that a read sees the latest acknowledged write?
blocks.exp: Strong consistency needs $R + W > N$. Here $2 + 3 = 5$, which is not greater than 5, so the read set and write set can be disjoint and the reader may miss the newest value. The other three give $6$, $6$ and $6$ respectively.

blocks.q: Which function may NOT be used as a MapReduce combiner without changing the result?
blocks.exp: A combiner runs the reduce logic on a partial, arbitrary subset of the values, so it is safe only when the operation is commutative and associative. Averaging an average of partial averages is wrong unless the counts are carried along; sum, max and count are all associative and safe.

blocks.q: According to the CAP theorem, a system that continues to serve reads and writes on both sides of a network partition has given up
blocks.exp: Serving both sides during a partition means the two sides can diverge, so a read is no longer guaranteed to see the most recent write — consistency is sacrificed. That is the AP design, as in Cassandra and DynamoDB; a CP system would instead refuse service on the minority side.

tricks.title: Number of mappers = number of input splits, not a parameter
tricks.body: Split size defaults to the HDFS block size, so mappers $= \lceil \text{file size} / \text{block size} \rceil$ per file. The reducer count *is* a parameter. Any question letting you choose the mapper count directly is testing this asymmetry.

tricks.title: CAP in one sentence: partitions are compulsory, so the real choice is C or A
tricks.body: Eliminate 'CA' as a distributed option immediately. Then classify by behaviour during a partition: refuses service $\Rightarrow$ CP; answers with possibly stale data $\Rightarrow$ AP.

tricks.title: $R + W > N$ is the whole quorum story
tricks.body: Compute the sum and compare with $N$. Greater means overlapping sets and strong consistency; equal or less means eventual consistency. $W > N/2$ additionally prevents two conflicting writes from both succeeding.

tricks.title: Key–value versus document = can you query inside the value
tricks.body: If the store can index and filter on fields *within* the stored object, it is a document store. If the value is an opaque blob retrievable only by its key, it is key–value. This single test separates the two families in any matching question.

tricks.title: Replication factor multiplies space, not block count
tricks.body: Blocks $= \lceil \text{size}/\text{blocksize}\rceil$ is independent of replication; replicas $= $ blocks $\times$ RF and disk $=$ size $\times$ RF. Keep the two numbers separate and the arithmetic never goes wrong.

traps.title: The C in CAP is not the C in ACID
traps.body: CAP's consistency is linearizability — every read sees the latest write across replicas. ACID's consistency is the preservation of application integrity constraints by a single transaction. A system can be ACID-consistent and CAP-inconsistent at the same time.

traps.title: The Secondary NameNode is not a backup NameNode
traps.body: It periodically checkpoints `fsimage` with the `edits` log to stop the journal growing without bound. It cannot take over if the NameNode fails; that requires the Hadoop 2 standby NameNode with a quorum journal and ZooKeeper failover.

traps.title: A partially filled HDFS block does not waste the rest of the block
traps.body: A 10 MB file in a 128 MB-block cluster occupies 10 MB of disk per replica, yet still counts as one block and still costs the NameNode a full metadata entry. The waste is in NameNode memory, not on the DataNode disks.

traps.title: NOSQL does not mean 'no transactions'
traps.body: Many document and wide-column stores offer atomic single-document or single-row operations, and several now support multi-document transactions. What they historically gave up is *distributed multi-object* ACID with joins, not atomicity as such.

traps.title: Spark transformations do nothing until an action runs
traps.body: A chain of `map` and `filter` calls only builds a DAG; no data moves until `count`, `collect` or a save is called. Questions asking 'at which line does execution occur' are testing lazy evaluation.
